An In-Silico Audit of Topographic Organization in a Multimodal Brain-Response Model

Jakub Strawa Affiliation: StrawAI, Krakow, Poland Email: jakubstrawaai@gmail.com
November 13, 2026
Abstract

TRIBE v2 (d’Ascoli et al., 2026) predicts fMRI responses across the cortical surface from video, audio and text. Its authors validated it with category-selective localizers (faces, places, bodies, words) and language contrasts, but not with the classic topographic organization of sensory cortex: retinotopy, tonotopy, and motion selectivity in area MT+. There is a clear architectural reason to expect retinotopy to fail: TRIBE’s video features are averaged over space before the response head, which should discard visual-field position. I present mapping stimuli, a fitting pipeline adapted from standard fMRI mapping analyses, and a stand-in model with known ground truth that serves as a positive and negative control, and apply them to TRIBE v2’s predictions, comparing the fitted maps with human atlases using spin tests. TRIBE v2 shows a sharp split. There is no contralateral hemifield response and no polar-angle map, robustly across stimulus controls. There is no tonotopic gradient in primary auditory cortex: best frequencies span an interquartile range of only 0.14 octaves across core and belt, and the null persists with loudness-equalized tones. An eccentricity-like gradient appears only when the ring geometry changes, consistent with global image statistics rather than a positional code. In contrast, motion selectivity is strong and precisely localized: 22% of the 1% most motion-selective vertices fall in MT+, which covers 0.42% of cortex. In-silico experiments that depend on feature identity appear viable with TRIBE v2, while those that depend on visual-field or frequency position are not supported by the current model.

1 Introduction

TRIBE v2 (d’Ascoli et al., 2026) is a foundation model trained to predict voxel/vertex-wise fMRI responses on the fsaverage5 cortical surface (20,484 vertices) from naturalistic video, audio and text input. Its original evaluation covered category-selective visual localizers (faces →\to FFA, places →\to PPA, bodies →\to EBA, words →\to VWFA) and language contrasts, where it performed well. It did not evaluate three of the best-replicated organizational principles in sensory neuroscience: retinotopy in early visual cortex, tonotopy in primary auditory cortex, and motion-selective responses in area MT+.

There is a specific architectural reason to expect retinotopy to fail: the paper’s own methods describe averaging V-JEPA 2 patch tokens over space before they reach the response head, which by construction removes the positional information a polar-angle or eccentricity map requires. No prior work has quantified whether this prediction holds, or whether motion selectivity (which does not depend on position, so should survive spatial averaging) and tonotopy (whose audio features are not pooled in the same way) fare differently.

I test four hypotheses, stated before running the model (Table 1):

Any outcome is informative: confirming H1 quantifies a concrete limitation for anyone using TRIBE for in-silico experiments that depend on visual-field position; disconfirming it would be a surprising finding about what spatially-averaged transformer features retain.

2 Methods

2.1 Stimuli

I generated the classic stimuli used to map each system experimentally: counter-rotating checkerboard wedges and expanding/contracting rings (retinotopy), a left/right hemifield flicker contrast, radially moving vs. static random-dot fields (motion), and ascending and descending logarithmic tone sweeps spanning 175 Hz–5.6 kHz in 10 six-semitone bands (tonotopy). Full stimulus parameters are in config.yaml of the project repository.11 1 https://github.com/jakubstrawa1/audit-multimodal-brain-response Figure 1 shows representative frames extracted from each stimulus video.

2.2 Model and inference

I ran the released facebook/tribev2 checkpoint (video encoder: V-JEPA 2 giant; audio encoder: Wav2Vec-BERT 2.0) on each stimulus, bypassing TRIBE’s text/transcription path entirely since no stimulus contains speech. Predictions were produced per-vertex at 1 Hz (TR = 1 s), with TRIBE’s built-in 5-second hemodynamic-lag correction already applied.

2.3 Fitting predicted responses

I fit the same models to TRIBE’s predicted time courses that are conventionally fit to real fMRI time courses:

  • •

    Retinotopy: a 2D Gaussian population receptive field (pRF; position and size) via grid search over wedge and ring responses jointly (Dumoulin and Wandell, 2008), plus Fourier power at the wedge frequency (ff) vs. twice that frequency (2​f2f) to separate position-coding from orientation-coding responses.

  • •

    Hemifield: contralateral −- ipsilateral response effect size.

  • •

    Motion: moving −- static response effect size.

  • •

    Tonotopy: Gaussian tuning curves on log frequency (best frequency, tuning width) fit jointly to ascending and descending sweeps.

An additional −3-3 to +8+8 s lag search was allowed on top of TRIBE’s built-in shift, since the model’s predicted auditory responses lag the stimulus by a further 2–3 s (Section 3.2).

2.4 Reference maps and null models

Fitted maps were compared against published human atlases on the same fsaverage5 mesh: the Benson retinotopy template for polar angle, eccentricity and V1–V3 boundaries (Benson et al., 2014; Benson and Winawer, 2018), the Glasser HCP-MMP parcellation for MT and MST (Glasser et al., 2016), and the posteromedial-to-anterolateral axis of A1 (the best-replicated human tonotopic gradient) for tonotopy (Saenz and Langers, 2014; Moerel et al., 2014). Because TRIBE is deterministic, there is no trial-to-trial sampling noise to test against; instead I ask whether a map’s spatial layout is aligned with known anatomy, using a spin test that rotates each map on the sphere while preserving its spatial autocorrelation (Alexander-Bloch et al., 2018), and, for tonotopy, a stimulus-label permutation that shuffles which frequency band is which.

2.5 Positive/negative control

Before running the real model, I validated the entire stimulus-generation, fitting and evaluation pipeline against a stand-in model with two configurable response modes: a retinotopic+tonotopic mode that plants known pRFs (from the Benson template) and an A1 frequency gradient, and a pooled+flat mode where visual vertices see only global image statistics (stimulated area, wedge orientation) and auditory vertices see only sound on/off – i.e., exactly what TRIBE’s architecture is expected to produce if H1 and H4 (null) hold. This lets me confirm the pipeline recovers a map when one is planted, and correctly reports its absence when it is not.

3 Results

3.1 Pipeline validation (stand-in model)

Table 2 confirms the analysis pipeline has the sensitivity and specificity needed to detect each type of map. The retinotopic+tonotopic stand-in recovers strong, significant contralaterality, polar-angle, and frequency-gradient effects; the pooled+flat stand-in – built to produce exactly the responses TRIBE’s architecture is expected to produce under H1/H4 – shows none of these effects (R1, R2, T1 near zero, R2b at chance), with the single exception of a weak, inconsistent eccentricity correlation (R3; significant in one of four random seeds), which is why eccentricity claims require the area-matched ring control (Section 4).

3.2 Tonotopy: TRIBE v2 predicts no tonotopic gradient

I ran the real TRIBE v2 model on the ascending and descending tone-sweep stimuli. Auditory cortex responds robustly to the tones: every core and belt vertex is well fit (T0: 100% clear the fit-quality threshold), and A1 is strongly suppressed during silence (z≈−2.1z\approx-2.1). However, I find no evidence of a tonotopic map: the spread of best frequencies across core and belt is only 0.141 octaves (T2), against 2.0 octaves in the planted-map stand-in control, and there is no gradient along A1 (T1: Spearman ρ=−0.067\rho=-0.067; spin p=0.418p=0.418; label-permutation p=0.343p=0.343). The posteromedial and anterolateral halves of A1 show near-identical band-by-band response profiles (Figure 3). This result was first observed in a smaller pilot run on the audio stimuli alone (T2 =0.14=0.14 octaves, ρ=−0.07\rho=-0.07) and is now confirmed on the full, six-stimulus run reported here – the numbers are essentially unchanged. Predicted responses peak 2–3 s later than TRIBE’s built-in 5-second hemodynamic-lag correction assumes, which I accommodate with the widened lag search described in Methods.

H4 verdict: no tonotopic gradient. H4 was stated as an open question; the answer is that TRIBE v2 predicts none. Because my main tones are equal in amplitude rather than in perceived loudness, the uniform best-frequency preference could partly reflect loudness. The headline finding does not depend on this, since every vertex is exposed to identical sounds, and the loudness-equalized control (Section 4) confirms that the gradient is still absent under equal loudness. I do not interpret the specific preferred frequency (∼\sim1.2 kHz) further.

3.3 Retinotopy: no positional code survives

Table 3 reports the full battery on real TRIBE v2 predictions for all four video stimuli. Fitted pRFs are well-behaved in the descriptive sense (R0: 100% of V1–V3 vertices clear the fit-quality threshold), but show no positional structure: the contralateral hemifield effect is near zero and non-significant (R1 d=0.048d=0.048, p=0.237p=0.237), polar angle does not correlate with the Benson template (R2 circular r=−0.024r=-0.024, p=0.595p=0.595), and eccentricity is, if anything, weakly negatively correlated with the template rather than positively (R3 Spearman =−0.129=-0.129, p=0.724p=0.724) at this default ring geometry – but this specific null is not stable: the area-matched and stimulus-size controls (Section 4) flip R3 to significant and positive (r=0.44r=0.44–0.760.76, p≤0.014p\leq 0.014) whenever the ring’s rendering geometry changes, while R1/R2/R2b stay robustly null throughout. I treat the eccentricity metric (R3) as unresolved rather than a clean null; see Section 4 and 5. R2b (fraction of pRFs landing in the geometrically correct contralateral hemifield) is 0.61, closer to chance (0.5) than to the stand-in positive control’s 1.0. Figure 4 makes this visible directly: the model’s fitted polar-angle and eccentricity maps are nearly uniform in color across V1–V3, in clear contrast to the smoothly varying template maps beside them.

One result complicates a fully clean null, however: R4 (the share of wedge-locked power at the stimulus frequency ff versus its first harmonic 2​f2f) is 0.744 – above the 0.5 midpoint and nominally in the “position-coding” direction, not the “orientation-coding” direction the interpretation key (Table 4) associates with a clean H1 confirmation. Taken together with R1–R3, I read this as: TRIBE v2’s predicted responses are phase-locked to the wedge’s periodic motion, but not in a way that decodes to a coherent, template-aligned polar-angle map – i.e., periodicity survives spatial averaging even though position does not. I discuss this discrepancy further in Section 5.

H1 verdict: confirmed for the position code H1 actually concerns – contralaterality and polar angle. No contralateral hemifield effect and no polar-angle map, robustly so across every control in Section 4 (ring geometry, wedge width, audio). This matches the architecture-level prediction that spatially-averaged video features cannot support a retinotopic code. Two caveats are carried forward rather than folded into the headline claim: R4 (above) and, more importantly, R3/eccentricity, which is not a stable null – it flips to significant and template-aligned whenever the ring’s rendering geometry changes (Section 4), consistent with the H2 prediction of an eccentricity-like signal driven by global image statistics rather than a true positional code. I treat eccentricity as an open question, not part of the confirmed H1 null.

H2 verdict: consistent with the prediction, in the “partly present” form stated in Table 1. There is no stable, geometry-invariant eccentricity code (R3 is null at the default ring geometry, and R1/R2/R2b show no positional code of any other kind), but an eccentricity-like signal appears whenever the ring geometry changes (Section 4), most plausibly carried by global image statistics that covary with that geometry.

3.4 Motion: TRIBE v2 correctly localizes motion selectivity to MT+

In clear contrast to retinotopy, the motion contrast is strong and precisely localized. The moving-minus-static effect size is large and significant both within MT+ (M1 d=4.31d=4.31, spin p=0.001p=0.001) and, more weakly, across the rest of cortex (M1b d=0.67d=0.67), but the top response is sharply concentrated: 22.0% of the single most motion-selective 1% of all cortical vertices fall inside the (anatomically tiny) MT+ parcel, a more than 50-fold enrichment over MT+’s 0.42% share of cortex (M2). Figure 5 shows the moving-static contrast map directly: a well-defined cluster in the expected posterolateral location on each hemisphere.

H3 verdict: confirmed. TRIBE v2 represents motion information, and the response is anatomically localized to the correct region, not merely present somewhere in cortex.

3.5 Hemifield contrast map

Figure 5 (left column) also shows the raw contralateral-minus-ipsilateral hemifield contrast map prior to V1–V3 masking; the diffuse, non-focal pattern across much of lateral and medial cortex is consistent with the null R1 statistic reported above and with the absence of a clean retinotopic code in early visual cortex specifically.

4 Controls and robustness

  1. 1.

    Silent audio vs. no audio. My video stimuli carry a silent audio track by default; I re-ran video experiments with the audio input dropped entirely. R1 and R2 remain non-significant with audio dropped (R1 d=0.045d=0.045, p=0.279p=0.279; R2 r=−0.031r=-0.031, p=0.540p=0.540; vs. d=0.048d=0.048, p=0.237p=0.237 and r=−0.024r=-0.024, p=0.595p=0.595 with audio present), so the retinotopic null is unaffected. The MT+ motion effect also survives (M1 d=3.25d=3.25, p=0.001p=0.001 vs. d=4.31d=4.31, p=0.001p=0.001 with audio), though both its effect size and its top-1%-vertex enrichment in MT+ roughly halve without the silent audio channel (M2 10.7% vs. 22.0%) – a real quantitative difference, but not one that changes which hypotheses are confirmed or disconfirmed.

  2. 2.

    Eccentricity vs. area. A ring control varying position while holding stimulated area constant tests whether the R3 result (Section 3.3) reflects position or area. Holding area constant does not null the effect: R3 becomes significant and positive (Spearman r=0.469r=0.469, p=0.014p=0.014), in contrast to the non-significant, slightly negative baseline (r=−0.129r=-0.129, p=0.724p=0.724). This rules out stimulated area alone as the explanation and is discussed together with the stimulus-size controls below.

  3. 3.

    Stimulus size. Repeating the analysis with max_ecc_deg of 5 and 20 (vs. the default 10) was expected to leave rank-based results unchanged. This holds for R1 and R2, which stay non-significant at both scales (R1 d=0.047d=0.047/0.0440.044, p=0.231p=0.231/0.2400.240; R2 r=0.028r=0.028/−0.0004-0.0004, p=0.497p=0.497/0.4780.478), but R3 becomes significant and positive at both — r=0.440r=0.440, p=0.012p=0.012 at 5° and r=0.755r=0.755, p=0.001p=0.001 at 20° — the same qualitative flip seen in the area control above. Across all three controls that regenerate the ring stimulus with altered geometry (area-matched, 5°, 20°), R3 flips from a non-significant, slightly negative baseline to a significant, positive, template-aligned correlation, while R1/R2/R2b stay robustly null throughout. I read this as consistent with the H2 prediction (an eccentricity-like gradient driven by global image statistics that covary with ring geometry) rather than a genuine, geometry-invariant positional code. Since the area-matched control already rules out stimulated area alone, other geometric properties (for example ring width, check size or proximity to the frame edge) are candidates; these controls do not identify which one is responsible – see the discussion of R3 in Section 3.3 and 5.

  4. 4.

    Wedge width and check size. Repeating the wedge experiment at 30° and 90° (vs. the default 45°) leaves H1’s central null intact: polar angle does not correlate with the template at either width (R2 r=−0.026r=-0.026, p=0.569p=0.569 at 30°; r=0.013r=0.013, p=0.557p=0.557 at 90°; vs. r=−0.024r=-0.024, p=0.595p=0.595 at 45°), and the R4 position-vs-orientation caveat (Section 3.3) persists essentially unchanged at all three widths (R4 =0.734=0.734, 0.7590.759, 0.7440.744 respectively).

  5. 5.

    Loudness-equalized tones. An ISO 226 equal-loudness version of the tone sweeps tests whether the missing gradient could be a loudness artifact (“best frequency = loudest frequency”; Section 3.2). The null persists under equal loudness: best frequency still does not track Heschl’s axis (Spearman r=−0.081r=-0.081, spin p=0.405p=0.405, label p=0.340p=0.340; vs. r=−0.067r=-0.067, spin p=0.418p=0.418, label p=0.343p=0.343 with equal-amplitude tones), confirming the absent tonotopic gradient is not a loudness artifact.

5 Discussion

Across all four hypotheses, TRIBE v2 shows a consistent pattern: codes that depend on where something is (visual-field position, tonotopic frequency position) are absent, while a code that depends on what kind of feature is present without requiring position (motion) survives and is correctly localized. H1 (retinotopy) is confirmed: as the architecture predicts, the spatially averaged video stream carries no usable positional code. H4 (tonotopy), stated as an open question, resolves as absent – more surprisingly, since the audio pathway has no equivalent spatial-pooling step. The tonotopic null therefore cannot be explained by the video pathway’s pooling. It may reflect what the model’s audio training data (mostly speech and film sound) taught it to represent, the audio encoder’s features, or how the response head aggregates sequence-level audio features; this audit does not distinguish between these. H3 (motion) is confirmed cleanly: MT+ selectivity is both strong and anatomically precise (M2), showing that TRIBE v2 can support in-silico experiments that depend on feature identity even in domains where position-dependent experiments fail.

The one result that resists a clean story is R4 (Section 3.3): wedge-locked periodic power is present (0.744, above the position-coding threshold) despite the complete absence of a coherent polar-angle map (R2) or contralaterality effect (R1). I see two readings. First, R4 may simply be a weaker, noisier signal than R1–R3: it requires only that some wedge-synchronized response exists somewhere in V1–V3, not that it be spatially organized, so it is a much lower bar to clear and may reflect overall stimulus-locked arousal/attention-like modulation rather than a retinotopic code. Second, it leaves open the possibility that some coarse spatial information survives averaging in a form the circular-correlation metric (R2) is not sensitive to – for instance, information about stimulated area or aggregate screen-side energy that correlates with wedge phase without reconstructing a true angular map. Distinguishing these two readings is a natural next step and does not change the paper’s central claim, since neither reading implies a usable positional (polar-angle or eccentricity) code.

R3 (eccentricity) shows a related pattern and is, if anything, a cleaner case of the same phenomenon: it is a non-significant, slightly negative null at the default ring geometry, but becomes a significant, template-aligned correlation under every control that regenerates the ring with different geometry (area-matched, 5°, 20°; Section 4). Because its sign and significance depend on how the ring is rendered, and holding stimulated area constant does not remove it, R3 does not behave like a stable positional code. I read it as consistent with the H2 prediction – an eccentricity-like gradient carried by global image statistics that covary with ring geometry – rather than evidence that TRIBE v2 retains true positional information, although these controls do not identify the statistic responsible, and a weak genuine eccentricity signal cannot be fully excluded. This matters for practitioners: an apparent eccentricity gradient in TRIBE v2’s predictions is not by itself evidence of a retinotopic code, and should be checked across several stimulus geometries before being interpreted.

For practitioners using TRIBE v2 for in-silico neuroscience, the practical implication is direct: experiments that depend on visual-field or tonotopic position (e.g., contralateral hemifield localizers, pRF mapping, frequency-selective auditory designs) should not be trusted with this model, while experiments that depend on category- or feature-level selectivity (as in the original paper’s face/place/body/word localizers, and as I demonstrate for motion) remain viable. For vision, the missing positional code is most likely architectural: the video features are averaged over space before the response head, so further training of the current design would not be expected to restore it, and a TRIBE version aiming to support position-based in-silico experiments would likely need to preserve spatial structure through to the response head. For audition the cause remains open, as discussed above. Ablations that modify the pooling step or the audio features are the natural way to test these explanations directly.

6 Limitations

  • •

    Resolution. fsaverage5 vertices are spaced approximately 4 mm apart; A1 comprises only about 45 vertices in total (22 left, 23 right) at this resolution, limiting sensitivity to fine-grained tonotopic structure.

  • •

    Average subject. TRIBE predicts a group-average subject’s response, so fitted maps are necessarily compared against group-level templates rather than individual-subject maps.

  • •

    Visual angle is undefined for TRIBE. I define the stimulus frame to span max_ecc_deg degrees (10 by default). The contralaterality and polar-angle tests (R1, R2) are unaffected by this choice, but the eccentricity correlation (R3) is not (Section 4), which is one reason R3 is treated as unresolved.

  • •

    Mechanisms are inferred, not tested. The architectural explanation for the visual null comes from the published model description; I did not modify the model to test it.

  • •

    Tonotopic axis. The orientation of tonotopic gradients relative to Heschl’s gyrus remains debated in the human-neuroimaging literature; T1 specifically tests the posteromedial-high/anterolateral-low pattern, while T2 (best-frequency spread) is direction-free.

This work used approximately 8 hours of H100 GPU time, including the control analyses, self-funded by the author with no external funding or grant support.
